To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) providing detailed information about the COVID 19 vaccine, including results of vaccine trials, does not significantly reduce perceptions that the vaccines are effective, concerns over side effect risks, or intentions to get vaccinated, (2) highlighting the need to continue protective behaviours post vaccination does not significantly reduce intentions to get vaccinated.

Providing transparent information about the effectiveness and side effects of COVID 19 vaccines did not reduce intentions to receive a vaccination, but also did not increase intentions to engage with protective behaviours post vaccination.
providing detailed information about COVID-19 vaccines does not have a negative impact on beliefs about efficacy, concerns over side-effects, or intentions to be vaccinated.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a dilemma faced by communicators in the context of a global health crisis: how to provide accurate information about the benefits of vaccination while also encouraging continued caution.
the impact of transparent communication about the limitations of vaccination on decision making.
the effects of transparent information on public health messaging.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of information about vaccine efficacy and side effects are small, and in the case of efficacy, non existent.
transparent communication about COVID 19 vaccinations has a negligible impact on behavioural intentions.
the results of these studies do not provide strong evidence for a significant impact of transparent communication on intentions to receive vaccination or protective behaviours post vaccination.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
providing information about the limitations of vaccines does not have an effect on intentions to be vaccinated.
transparent information about the efficacy of vaccines does not undermine intentions to be vaccinated, but neither does it encourage protective behaviour post vaccination.
providing transparent and balanced information does not have negative effects, but does not increase intentions to be vaccinated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
transparent communication does not appear to have a negative impact on intentions to engage in health protective behaviours, and may have a positive effect on some measures of vaccine efficacy.
the provision of transparent information about vaccines does not appear to reduce intentions to receive a COVID 19 vaccine.
transparently communicating the limitations and uncertainties of vaccines does not appear to undermine intentions to receive a vaccination.
